extracted.intended_audience: NLP / ML researchers and practitioners working on multimodal humor generation and captioning
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and methodological standards for designing, training, and measuring multimodal humor (image) captioning systems, including dataset curation, algorithmic modularity, automatic and human-centered metrics, and safety checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three humor-theory-driven modules (D, C, Tim)
rubrics_metrics.description: A multi-role framework employs three coordinated roles: a conflict-script extractor (C) that identifies detailed situation descriptions and script oppositions, a hierarchical imaginator (Tim) that stimulates imaginative associations with retrieval, and a situation description (D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing any single module consistently degrades performance, verifying the necessity of D, C, Tim in multi-modal caption generation. The largest performance drop seen in I+D+Tim highlights the significance of conflict script C as a basis of caption generation. Inadequate guidance of imagination leads to performance drops and may produce irrelevant or nonsensical captions. The modular design enables explicit control over humor logic and materials, targeted editing, and improved creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor-relevance score H(·) (relevance-opposition, frequency, diversity)
rubrics_metrics.description: H(·) combines three components — relevance-opposition (semantic relevance and conceptual opposition), frequency (how often a token/concept appears in related jokes), and diversity — to score candidate imagination elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ablations show removing the relevance term ('w/o relevance') causes a significant performance drop, validating the need to model semantic relevance and conceptual opposition. The w/o frequency and w/o diversity variants also degrade performance, indicating all three components are useful for exploring imagination. Calculation details: H(e) = Hrel + Hfreq + Hdiv with specific TSS/CO and counting terms as in the algorithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unbiased pass@k metric
rubrics_metrics.description: pass@k estimates the probability that at least one of k randomly selected captions is funnier than the human-written caption. For each image, sample n candidate captions, let c be the number that are funnier than the ground truth; use the unbiased pass@k formula (correcting for multiple winners among samples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formula corrects for bias when multiple winner captions exist. In experiments ni is set to 5. Use averaging over all N images to compute overall pass@k. This is the primary automatic metric reported (pass@1, pass@3, pass@5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Human funniness rating protocol (5-point scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human evaluation uses a five-point funniness rating rule: 1: not funny, 2: slightly funny, 3: moderately funny, 4: funny, 5: very funny. Raters score captions according to this scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper used 20 raters and obtained 5600 rating scores. Mean ratings (± std) are reported per method. A mean score > 3.0 indicates captions judged to be over moderately funny. Inter-rater agreement is reported with Cohen's kappa (κ = 0.49 in this study) — consider κ values in context of inherent subjectivity; κ ≈ 0.49 was described as an acceptable level of agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmful content detection across seven toxicity dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate generated captions with Detoxify across seven dimensions: toxicity, severe_toxicity, obscene, identity_attack, insult, threat, and sexual_explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report average scores per dataset and summed toxicity; low sums (e.g., sum < 0.03 on Humor in AI and sum ≈ 0.015 on Electronic Sheep reported here) indicate negligible harmful content. Use these scores to claim avoidance of abusive, threatening, or sexually explicit language. Provide appendix with more detailed detection results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness to hyperparameters k and δ (number of retrieved jokes and humor-relevant entities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two retrieval hyperparameters govern imagination: number of retrieved jokes k and number of humor-relevant entities threshold δ. Both are tested across values [3, 5, 7, 9].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results indicate stability across the tested range. Empirically, retrieving too few (small k) yields insufficient imagination space; retrieving too many introduces noise (unrelated entities). The study selects k = 5 and δ = 5 to balance performance and noise. Report robustness plots (Figures 4/5) and include appendix analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization across visual domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess model performance on diverse image domains (realistic, comic, cartoon, synthetic) using an external meme dataset (ImgFlip / Memecap) and compare generated captions against ground-truth meme captions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HOMER outperformed strong competitors by ≈5.4% on average on the meme data, validating cross-domain generalization. When evaluating generalization, explicitly test on datasets with differing visual styles and report pass@k or other metrics per domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset curation and licensing policy for humor retrieval DB
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct humor retrieval database via multi-stage curation: collect public humor datasets, filter by internal humor ratings to remove jokes rated < 3, clean noise, remove duplicates and near-duplicates (>80% word overlap keep longer), and exclude multimodal datasets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict corpus to text-only one-liner jokes; exclude any datasets used for multimodal applications to prevent cross-modal leakage. After curation the study reports a retrieval database of 335,570 jokes. Follow clear provenance and licensing rules; provide a table summarizing formats, sources, and intended use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of modalities between database and test set
rubrics_metrics.description: The joke database is text-only (one-liners) and explicitly excludes cartoons/image captions; the test set is multimodal (e.g., New Yorker Caption Contest captions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the text-only DB for text-only humor tasks (detection/rating/generation) and reserve multimodal captioning evaluation for the multimodal test set to avoid modality leakage and unfair overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributional analysis of script-opposition types (humor bases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterize the dataset by types of script-opposition / humor basis: Abnormalities, Unexpected logic, Contextual incongruity, Exaggeration, Ambiguity, Personification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report counts and percentages per category (example: Abnormalities 34%, Unexpected Logic 19%, Contextual Incongruity 18%, Exaggeration 14%, Ambiguity 15% in the Humor in AI dataset). Use these dimensions to analyze model strengths/weaknesses by humor type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-dimensional qualitative/quantitative evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate multimodal humor generation across four key dimensions: (1) visual understanding, (2) humor understanding, (3) humor imagination, and (4) stylistic expression, using both expert LLMs (GPT-5) and automated metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide both qualitative case studies and quantitative scores/tables for each dimension (Tables 11/12 referenced). Use expert LLM judgements alongside human raters and automated metrics to capture different aspects of humor quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of humor-frequency scoring vs TF-IDF
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast the proposed humor-frequency weighting (which up-weights tokens/concepts recurring in jokes relevant to a situation and its conflicting scripts) with TF-IDF (which down-weights globally common tokens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective differs: aim to identify salient, frequently used humor components rather than penalize global commonness. Ablation/experiments show humor-frequency outperforms TF-IDF on pass@k (e.g., pass@1 TF-IDF 63.00 vs Humor-Frequency 66.41). Include such baselines when arguing for scoring choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness to LLM sampling temperature
rubrics_metrics.description: Test stability under different sampling temperatures (T ∈ {0, 0.5, 1}) for the LLM used in imagination/generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report performance across temperatures (Figure 8). The method here achieved consistently strong performance across tested temperatures, indicating the approach is not sensitive within this range — report such robustness checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-phase algorithmic design/verification (Phase I/II/III)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design and describe the system in three phases: Phase I Script Extraction (Extract C and D), Phase II Imagination (Tim — initialize targets, deep-pattern imagination via LLM associations, humor-relevance retrieval to build imagination trees), Phase III Generation (GTVH-guided generator conditioned on constructed knowledge resources).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide algorithmic pseudocode (Algorithm 1), detail intermediate outputs (e.g., chosen conflicting scripts, imagination paths, selected targets), and demonstrate traceable imagination paths in case studies. Verify via ablations that each phase/module contributes meaningfully to final performance.
